steps.prompt: Training's done — now what do you actually DO with it?
steps.sub: When training finishes you get a 'policy' — the robot's learned brain. By the end you'll know how to export it, render it to watch, and tell a good policy from a clumsy one at a glance.

steps.prompt: First instinct — training just finished. What did you actually end up with?

options.t: A video file of the robot, ready to post online.
A trained policy — a saved 'brain' that maps what the robot senses to the action it should take.
Nothing reusable; you'd have to retrain from scratch every time you want the robot to move.

steps.why: The output of RL training is a policy: a saved function (often a small neural network) that takes the robot's observation and returns an action. It's the learned skill itself — you can export it once and reuse it forever to control the robot, in sim or on real hardware, without retraining.
hints: RL trains a decision-maker. What's the saved form of that decision-maker called?
It maps observation → action. That mapping is the thing you keep.

steps.prompt: From trained policy to something you can watch.
steps.sub: Tap each card. Three steps turn a checkpoint into a video.

cards.b: Save the policy to a portable file (e.g. ONNX) so it runs outside the training setup — in a renderer, sim, or on the robot.
Run the policy in the simulator: feed it observations, let it pick actions, and record the robot's motion frame by frame.
Turn that recorded run into a video (MP4) so you — and a human reviewer — can actually SEE how the robot behaves.

steps.prompt: Tap the deploy-and-watch steps in the order you'd run them.
chips: Render the recorded motion into an MP4 you can watch
Export the trained policy to a portable file
Roll out the policy in the simulator and record each frame
hints: You can't run a policy you haven't exported out of the trainer yet.
Export → roll out (record) → render the recording to video.

steps.prompt: You watch the rendered clip. Sort each thing you see: good policy, or bad policy?
steps.sub: Tap an item, then tap a bin. This is exactly how a reviewer eyeballs a run.

items.t: Robot walks smoothly and reaches the goal post
Robot trembles, vibrates, and never settles
Robot dives forward and face-plants for speed
Robot moves with steady, efficient, natural-looking steps
Robot spins in place and never makes progress

hints: Good = reaches the goal, looks smooth and natural, stays upright.
Bad = the reward-hacking and jitter symptoms: diving, trembling, spinning, never arriving.

steps.prompt: Your robot reaches the goal in the clip — but it twitches violently the whole way and looks like it's seizing. What does this most likely mean?
steps.sub: A good policy isn't just 'did it arrive'.

options.t: It's a great policy — arriving is all that matters.
The reward rewarded reaching the goal but not smooth motion, so the policy is jerky — likely worth a smoothness penalty and a retrain.
The render is broken; the policy is definitely perfect.

steps.why: Reaching the goal is necessary but not sufficient. Violent twitching usually means the reward didn't penalize jerky, high-energy motion — so the policy found a thrashy way to get there. A jittery real robot wears out motors and is unsafe, so you'd add a smoothness term and retrain. This is why we WATCH, not just read the reward number.
hints: Did the reward say anything about HOW it should move, or only that it should arrive?
Twitchy motion is a classic sign of a missing smoothness penalty.

steps.prompt: Walk through a real deploy-and-review session, end to end.
steps.sub: At each step, pick the right next move. The log fills in as you go.
steps.goal: Take a freshly trained walking policy and decide if it's ready to ship.

turns.situation: Training just finished and saved a checkpoint of the policy.
turns.q: What's your FIRST move to get it ready to use?
options: Export the policy to a portable file like ONNX

turns.situation: The policy is exported. You want to see it actually move.
options: Roll it out in the simulator and record the motion
Guess how it looks from the reward number alone
Ship it straight to a real robot, unseen
turns.log: ▶️ Roll out in sim → motion recorded.

turns.situation: You have a recorded run sitting in the simulator's memory.
turns.q: How do you actually watch it?
options: Render the recording into an MP4 and play it
Read the raw numbers and imagine the video

turns.situation: You watch the clip: the robot walks smoothly and stops right at the goal post.
options: Good policy — smooth, upright, reaches the goal → ship it
Bad policy — it didn't crash, so it must be broken
Inconclusive — you can't judge a policy by watching it

hints: Remember the pipeline: export → roll out → render → watch and judge.
A good run looks smooth, stays upright, and reaches the goal.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: A trained policy can be exported once and reused to control the robot without retraining.
statements.why: Right — the policy is the saved skill. Export it (e.g. to ONNX) and run it anytime to control the robot in sim or reality.

statements.t: Reaching the goal is enough to call a policy good, regardless of how it moves.
statements.why: No — a policy that arrives by twitching violently or diving is still bad. Smooth, stable, efficient motion matters for safety and real hardware.

statements.t: Rendering the policy to a video lets a human actually SEE behavior the reward number hides.
statements.why: Yes — the reward number can look great while the motion looks awful. Watching the rendered clip catches reward-hacking and jitter the number misses.

statements.t: The very first trained policy is usually the final one — you rarely need another round.
statements.why: No — watching the clip often reveals a problem (jitter, diving, falling short), sending you back to tweak the reward and retrain. Deploy-and-watch closes the loop.

hints: Think about what 'export' buys you, and whether arriving alone makes a policy good.
Why bother rendering at all? Because numbers can lie about how movement LOOKS.

steps.sub: Not graded. This ties the whole pipeline back to a robot you'd actually want to ship.

fields.label: Think of the robot task you'd most want to train and watch. When you press play on the clip, what does SUCCESS look like?
fields.ph: e.g. it walks across the room and sets the cup down gently, no spill

fields.label: What would you see in the video that tells you 'not ready — go back and fix the reward'?
fields.ph: e.g. it gets there but jerks and slams the cup down
